findings.title: The ContractAddresses interface regenerated by `dev` makes PhlimboV3, Kendu and NudgeStreamer required mainnet keys that are satisfied by zero-address placeholders, and the local rehearsal cannot surface it
findings.severityNote: Proposed Low. This is an off-chain UI artifact, not on-chain funds, and the placeholder convention is documented in-file — which cuts toward 'obvious'. It is escalated above pure QA because it is the precise failure mode of stated purpose (b), and because the type system reports GREEN over it. severity-classifier to weigh.
findings.description: `generate:ts-anvil` regenerates `server/deployments/addresses.ts` — the `ContractAddresses` interface — from the LOCAL anvil deployment. `server/deployments/mainnet-addresses.ts` imports that interface and annotates `export const mainnetAddresses: ContractAddresses`. So a local anvil run defines the compile-time contract the hand-maintained mainnet address book is validated against. The coupling itself currently HOLDS: `tsc --noEmit --strict` exits 0 against the just-regenerated interface, and all 55 interface keys are present on the mainnet object (the three `Burner*` keys that look like excess properties are commented out at lines 105-109). The defect is HOW it holds. Three keys — `PhlimboV3`, `Kendu`, `NudgeStreamer` — are required `string` on the interface and carry `"0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000000"` on mainnet. The file's own comment is candid about it: 'zero-address placeholders keep this hand-maintained file's key-set equal to the regenerated interface (tsc drift guard). Patch by hand when they ship.' `string` cannot distinguish a real address from a zero one, so the drift guard passes while three of the newest and most load-bearing contracts resolve to address(0). Critically, `dev` is STRUCTURALLY INCAPABLE of surfacing this: on the local chain all three resolve to live, funded contracts (PhlimboV3 holding 300e18 of migrated stake, Kendu with an armed 10,000-token promotion, NudgeStreamer with three funded buffers). The rehearsal that exists to prepare the UI for mainnet validates the SHAPE of the address book and never its VALUES.
findings.impact: A UI built against this interface compiles and type-checks clean while three mainnet lookups return address(0). Depending on the call site that is a silent no-op read (a dormant-looking farm), or a write to the zero address. The enforcement that prevents it is a code comment saying 'patch by hand when they ship' — and the only automated rehearsal in the project cannot fail on it, because locally the values are always populated. This is squarely the audit's grading bar: a local shortcut that makes the rehearsal succeed where mainnet would not.
findings.evidence: evidence/tsc-mainnet-addresses.log (tsc --strict exit 0); evidence/addresses.ts (55 required keys); evidence/mainnet-addresses.ts lines 53/78/142; evidence/local-addresses.ts + evidence/local.json (0 zero-addresses locally); evidence/live-state-fork-test.log (all three live on the local chain)
findings.recommendation: Make the placeholder visible to the type system rather than hidden by it. Either (a) type pending keys as a distinct branded type or `string | null` so every consumer is forced to handle the not-yet-deployed case, or (b) — cheaper and no ABI churn — add a `scripts/check-mainnet-addresses.js` gate that fails on any `0x0{40}` value and wire it into the `promotion-ready:dry` / `promotion-ready:broadcast` preamble, so the cutover cannot broadcast while the address book still advertises placeholders. Additionally, have `generate:ts-anvil` emit a comment block listing which mainnet keys are currently zero, so the drift is reported at the moment the interface is regenerated.

findings.title: clean:local deletes the JSON deployment artifacts but leaves addresses.ts / local-addresses.ts stale, so the in-repo consumer fails loudly while the external UI consumer fails silently
findings.description: `clean:local` is `rm -rf broadcast/*/31337 server/deployments/progress.31337.json server/deployments/local.json && rm -rf ~/.foundry/anvil/tmp/*`. It does NOT delete `server/deployments/addresses.ts` or `server/deployments/local-addresses.ts` — the two TypeScript artifacts the external UI repo actually imports. On any chain that aborts after the clean (and the clean runs first in both job 1 and again inside `deploy:local`), the workspace is left with NO JSON and STALE TypeScript. Demonstrated empirically: after running `clean:local` against a completed deployment, `progress.31337.json` and `local.json` were gone and `broadcast/DeployMocks.s.sol/31337` was removed, while `local-addresses.ts` was byte-identical (sha256 prefix c8e0355fbc73, unchanged) and still named `PhlimboV3: "0xC32609C91d6B6b51D48f2611308FEf121B02041f"`. The asymmetry is the finding, and it runs the wrong way round: the JSON consumers inside this repo fail LOUDLY and correctly — `server/index.js` re-reads both files on every request, so `/health` honestly flipped to `deploymentsLoaded:false` and `/contracts` returned HTTP 404 — but the TypeScript consumer, which is the external UI repo and therefore the entire point of stated purpose (b), has no staleness signal whatsoever. It simply imports addresses for contracts that no longer exist on any chain.
findings.impact: A developer whose `npm run dev` aborted mid-chain, or who re-cleaned without redeploying, has a UI that builds and runs against addresses from a previous anvil session. On a fresh anvil those addresses are code-less; on a re-run they are frequently the same deterministic CREATE addresses for a DIFFERENT deployment generation, which is worse — the UI appears to work while reading a contract that is not the one it thinks it is. This is the concealment case the local-testing framing does not excuse.
findings.evidence: evidence/clean-local-stale-ts-demo.log (before/after sha256 of all four artifacts, plus the /health and /contracts responses)
findings.recommendation: Add `server/deployments/addresses.ts server/deployments/local-addresses.ts` to the `clean:local` rm list, so an aborted run leaves nothing rather than something stale. If the .ts files must survive for editor tooling, instead have `generate:ts-anvil` stamp a run id (block hash or timestamp) into both files and have the UI bootstrap assert it against `GET /health` — but deletion is simpler and fails in the safe direction.

findings.title: `dev` rehearses the cutover's end state but not its cutover mechanics: setDispatcher, replaceDispatcher and hook.pull() are executed zero times
findings.severityNote: Proposed Low. Under strict C4 a rehearsal-coverage gap is QA/Low — no deployed code is defective and no assets are at risk. It is filed prominently because the requester's stated purpose (a) is exactly 'test the whole sequence of cutovers', and this is the headline defect against it.
findings.description: `DeployMainnetPromotionReady.s.sol` calls `setDispatcher` 9 times, `replaceDispatcher` 9 times and `hook.pull()` at least 3 times. `DeployMocks.s.sol` calls each of them ZERO times. Verified on the live chain: `NFTMinterV2.nextIndex == 8` with `configs[1..7]` each populated exactly once and never repointed — the local chain deploys the post-cutover dispatcher set greenfield, because it has no incumbent to displace. The mainnet script documents the per-index order at `:145-156` — `hook.pull() -> hook.setDispatcher(new) -> new.setHook(hook) -> replaceDispatcher(idx, new)` — and states in its own words that the reverse order 'would put the new dispatcher live on the index while it still carried the fresh DefaultDispatchHook that ATokenDispatcherV2's constructor gave it, so mints would SUCCEED while accruing no mint debt — a silent value leak. Never do that.' The one ordering in the whole cutover whose wrong direction is SILENT rather than loud is the one the local mirror never executes. The same omission also means these mainnet claims are never exercised locally: that `replaceDispatcher` preserves `price`/`growthBasisPoints` (asserted at `:1366-1372` and `:1536`); that `NudgeRatchet._dispatch`'s `hookTypeId() == EXPECTED_HOOK_TYPE_ID` guard holds across a hook reuse; and that `NudgeRatchetMintDebtHook`'s non-default `DEFAULT_RATIO == 100` is not silently reset. Two adjacent cutover behaviours are likewise absent with no analogue: old-batch-minter retirement (`setPauser(OWNER)` + `pause()`), and the story-074 write-once BPT custody baseline / resume-leg handling — the latter structurally un-rehearsable because `DeployMocks` writes `deploymentStatus: "completed"` unconditionally and can never record `in_progress` or `failed`.
findings.impact: A reordering regression in the mainnet cutover script — the exact defect class the mainnet script's own comment flags as a silent value leak — would pass the local rehearsal unchanged, because the local rehearsal contains none of the calls involved. The rehearsal's green result therefore carries less assurance than it appears to, which is the concealment bar. No claim is made that the mainnet ordering IS wrong; the finding is that `dev` cannot tell you either way.
findings.evidence: grep counts over both scripts (setDispatcher 0 vs 9, replaceDispatcher 0 vs 9); evidence/cast-live-state.log (NFTMinterV2 nextIndex=8, configs[1..7] all greenfield); evidence/dev-script-narrative.log (25 phases, none of them a repoint); reports/.../script-audits/dev/cluster-analysis.md G-1/G-2/G-3
findings.notDemonstratedByExecution: The reverse-order leak was NOT reproduced on the live chain — doing so would have required deploying a fresh six-arg BalancerPoolerV2 plus hook and repointing index 4. The ABSENCE of the calls is proven; the consequence of getting the order wrong is quoted from the mainnet script's own documentation, not independently demonstrated here.
findings.recommendation: Add a Phase 7.6 to `DeployMocks.s.sol` that, after the greenfield dispatcher set is live, deploys ONE replacement dispatcher and performs a genuine `hook.pull() -> hook.setDispatcher(new) -> new.setHook(hook) -> replaceDispatcher(idx, new)` on a single index, asserting (i) mint-debt conservation across the swap, (ii) `price`/`growthBasisPoints` preserved, and (iii) that a mint attempted in the intermediate window REVERTS rather than succeeding. One index is sufficient to make the ordering executable and therefore regression-testable. Separately, run `VerifyPromotionReady.s.sol` (story 075) against the local end state — it is free there, and story 075 closed via machine approval with its own declared regression gate never run.

findings.title: The local chain arms a Kendu promotion that story 076 asserts must be dormant on mainnet, and never produces the dormant state the UI will actually ship against
findings.description: `_armLocalKenduPromotion` arms a 10,000-Kendu / 1-day promotion on PhlimboV3. Verified live: `promoToken == MockKendu`, `promoPhase == Active (1)`, `promoRewardBalance == 10,000e18`, `promoRewardPerSecond == 1.157e35`. Story 076 asserts the exact opposite for mainnet — `promoToken == address(0)`, Kendu deliberately unset, Phase 7 asserting the negative — and `DeployMainnetPromotionReady.s.sol` calls `startPromotion` nowhere. THE ARMING ITSELF IS ADMISSIBLE and is not the finding: it is declared deliberate at `:183-198`, argued well (with no promotion running, every new V3 UI field — 13/16/17/18/19 plus the three unclaimable banks on DepositPageViewV3 — reads zero, which is indistinguishable from a broken binding), and carefully sequenced dead-last so the migrator's `promoToken`-delta path stays dormant during the migration. The finding is the INVERSE: because the promotion is armed unconditionally at the end of every local run, no local run ever produces the DORMANT promo state that mainnet will actually ship on day one. The UI's dormant-promotion rendering path is the one path `dev` never exercises, and it is the path that goes live first. Compounding it, `mainnet-addresses.ts` carries `Kendu: "0x000…0"` (see DEV26-01), so a UI developer working against `dev` sees an active promotion on a live Kendu token where mainnet will present a dormant promotion on the zero address. Note per project policy that the in-source comment declaring this deliberate is evidence of intent, not suppression authority.
findings.impact: The day-one mainnet UI state — dormant promo, zero-address Kendu — is the single state the local rehearsal cannot produce, so any rendering bug specific to it (a zero-division on `promoRewardPerSecond`, a null-token symbol lookup, a banner that renders 'promotion active' off a non-zero `promoPhase` enum) ships unrehearsed. This is a purpose-(b) blind spot created by an otherwise-sound purpose-(b) shortcut.
findings.evidence: evidence/live-state-fork-test.log (test_B: promoToken/promoPhase/promoBalance read live); evidence/dev-script-narrative.log (the four require-based post-conditions at :1913-1916 all passing); DeployMocks.s.sol:183-198 and :1902-1921
findings.recommendation: Make both promo states reachable locally. Cheapest: gate the call on an env flag (`LOCAL_PROMO=off` skips `_armLocalKenduPromotion`) so a developer can boot the dormant chain on demand. Better: add a follow-on local phase that ends the promotion after arming it, so a single `npm run dev` produces the armed state AND leaves a documented one-command path to the dormant/depleted state. Either way, keep the four non-vacuous post-condition requires — they are correct and should not be relaxed.

findings.title: DeployMocks.s.sol has no require(block.chainid == 31337) while AddressLoader.sol added exactly that guard in the same delta
findings.description: RE-OBSERVATION, STILL-LIVE, with a new aggravating fact. `block.chainid` appears exactly once in the 2,337-line script, inside a `console.log("Chain ID:", block.chainid)` at `:365`. There is no `require(block.chainid == 31337)`. The repo's own CLAUDE.md mandates that anvil relaxations 'must be gated behind an explicit block.chainid == 31337 branch', and this script is composed almost entirely of such relaxations — permissionless mock mints, a self-granted phUSD minter role, an armed promotion, deployer-donor seeding. The new fact this run: `script/interactions/AddressLoader.sol` ADDED exactly such a require in this same delta, with the rationale 'on mainnet that is an approve/transfer to a stranger's contract'. The pattern was available, understood and applied to a sibling in the same commit, and not applied here. Practical exposure is genuinely bounded — `deploy:local` hardcodes `--rpc-url http://localhost:8545` — so this is a defence-in-depth gap rather than a live hazard. But the script also hardcodes the STRING `"chainId": 31337` into `_writeProgressFile` and into its output filename, so a run against any other chain would produce artifacts that confidently mislabel their own provenance, and `extract-addresses.js` / `generate-ts-addresses.js` would consume them without complaint.
findings.impact: Defence-in-depth only, given the hardcoded RPC. The concrete residual is artifact mislabelling: output that asserts chain 31337 regardless of the chain it came from, feeding a toolchain whose next step writes the mainnet UI's type contract.
findings.evidence: grep -n chainid script/DeployMocks.s.sol (single hit, line 365, inside console.log); script/interactions/AddressLoader.sol (guard added this delta); evidence/progress.31337.json (hardcoded chainId string)
findings.recommendation: Add `require(block.chainid == 31337, "DeployMocks: anvil only")` as the first statement of `run()`, matching `AddressLoader.sol`. Separately, derive the progress file's `chainId` field and filename from `block.chainid` rather than hardcoding the literal, so artifacts cannot misreport their origin.

findings.title: The deploy script grants itself phUSD mint authority and never revokes it, while correctly revoking PhlimboV2's grant in the same run
findings.description: `phUSD.setMinter(deployer, true)` is granted at `:1784`, `:2025` and `:2122` and is never revoked. Verified live at the end of the run: `phUSD.authorizedMinters(0xf39Fd6e51aad88F6F4ce6aB8827279cffFb92266) == (true, 1)`. The grant is a legitimate local shortcut — the deployer acts as a synthetic donor to seed the phUSD nudge stream, which story 073 sanctions — and the token is a mock on a chain whose keys are public, so there is no local risk. The finding is the inconsistency and what it costs the rehearsal: the SAME script, in the SAME run, correctly revokes PhlimboV2's grant as an explicit ordered step of the Phase 7.4 wind-down (verified: `authorizedMinters(PhlimboV2) == (false, 1)`, `authorizedMinters(PhlimboV3) == (true, 1)`), and logs it as such. So privilege revocation is clearly understood as a first-class cutover step here — just not applied to the deployer's own grant. Consequently the local chain's end state carries a live minter that mainnet's end state must not, and the 'revoke the operational key's temporary grant' step is never rehearsed even though it is precisely the kind of step that is easy to forget on a Ledger broadcast.
findings.impact: No local risk (mock token, public anvil key). The cost is rehearsal fidelity: a residual-privilege sweep is never exercised, and the local end state differs from the intended mainnet end state in a way no assertion catches. This is an owner footgun of the non-obvious kind — the script's own careful revocation of the OTHER grant makes it read as though residual privileges were swept.
findings.recommendation: Revoke the deployer's grant at the end of `run()` with `phUSD.setMinter(deployer, false)` and assert it, mirroring the Phase 7.4 wind-down's own pattern. Better still, add a terminal 'residual privilege sweep' phase that asserts the full expected end-state ACL — deployer not a minter, PhlimboV2 not a minter, PhlimboV3 a minter — so the check is declarative and a future grant that forgets to clean up fails the run.

findings.title: GET / advertises a hand-maintained availableContracts array that has drifted to 17 entries against 55 actual, naming three contracts that do not exist
findings.description: `GET /` returns a static documentation JSON whose `availableContracts` array is hand-maintained. Verified live against the same running server whose `/contracts` returns 55 keys: the array lists 17 entries, of which THREE do not exist on the chain at all — `USDT`, `YieldStrategyUSDT`, `YieldStrategyUSDS` — and it omits `PhlimboV3`, `NudgeStreamer`, `ViewRouter`, `StableStaker`, `BatchNFTMinter` and the entire NFT/Uniboost/ratchet stack. Every contract introduced by the promotion-ready cutover work is missing from the discovery surface that documents the API. Story 078 edited this exact array in this delta (removing `DepositView`) without correcting the drift, so it was touched and left wrong.
findings.impact: A UI developer using `GET /` as the contract discovery surface — which is what it is for — is told the local chain has USDT and two yield strategies it does not have, and is not told it has PhlimboV3, the NudgeStreamer or the ViewRouter. Low impact because `/contracts` is authoritative and correct, but it is documentation that actively misdescribes the rehearsal, against stated purpose (b).
findings.recommendation: Delete the hand-maintained array and derive it from the loaded `local.json` at request time — the data is already in memory on the same code path that serves `/contracts`. A hand-maintained mirror of a generated list has no way to stay correct and, as story 078 showed, gets edited without being reconciled.

findings.title: BatchNFTMinterMultiToken.setNudgeStreamer accepts address(0) while all five donor contracts reject it, silently stranding funded stream buffers
findings.description: RE-OBSERVATION, STILL-LIVE (this is very likely run-21's setNudgeStreamer finding — orchestrator to map). All five donor contracts guard the setter: `BalancerPoolerV2:247`, `NudgeRatchet:106`, `Uniboost:191` each `require(newStreamer != address(0))`, and `StableYieldAccumulator:514` reverts `ZeroAddress()`. The SINK does not: `BatchNFTMinterMultiToken.setNudgeStreamer` at `:297-300` emits and assigns with no check. This is deliberate and documented — `:198-203` states `address(0)` disables the integration, 'keeping the whole feature optional/backward-safe', and `batchMint:529-535` reads `if (_nudgeStreamer != address(0))` before looping `pullPendingStream`. So it is a designed sentinel, not an oversight, and it is filed as a footgun rather than a bug. The footgun: once streams are registered AND FUNDED, zeroing the sink makes every accrued buffer unreachable through the normal path with no revert and no distinguishing event — `batchMint` simply stops flushing and keeps succeeding. Verified on the live chain, which had three funded buffers at the time (USDC 44870110 at 6dp, phUSD 5,000e18, Kendu 50,000e18): `setNudgeStreamer(address(0))` was ACCEPTED and `nudgeStreamer()` read back as the zero address. The asymmetry is what makes it non-obvious — an operator who has learned from five donors that this setter rejects zero will not expect the sixth to accept it.
findings.impact: An owner disabling streaming on a funded sink strands the buffers with no error surfaced; `batchMint` continues to succeed while paying out a smaller pot, so the symptom is under-payment rather than a revert. Recovery requires re-pointing the sink, which is possible — funds are not permanently lost — so impact is bounded. Reported as a non-obvious owner footgun (Law 3), not as a malicious-owner vector.
findings.evidence: evidence/live-state-fork-test.log (test_D, run forked against the live anvil with a code-length tripwire in setUp so it cannot pass vacuously); source comparison of the six setters
findings.recommendation: Keep the sentinel — the optional-integration design is sound — but make the transition explicit rather than silent. Require a distinct call (`disableNudgeStreaming()`) to reach the zero state, or `require` that every registered stream's buffer is zero before allowing the sink to be zeroed, so an operator who is about to strand funded buffers is told so. At minimum emit a distinguishable event on the zeroing transition rather than reusing `NudgeStreamerChanged`.
findings.dedupNote: Almost certainly maps to the run-21 'silent setNudgeStreamer' finding (recorded in project memory as run-21 M-02). Orchestrator must confirm the fingerprint rather than minting a new one.

findings.title: The un-storied 'Story 079' work has no acceptance criteria anywhere to be graded against
findings.description: LAW-2 FINDING, STATED PLAINLY. `script/DeployMocks.s.sol` references 'Story 079' ten times and `script/interactions/AddressLoader.sol` once more. Globbing the entire phStaging2 story tree across all state folders (`complete`, `incomplete`, `review`, `auto-complete`) for `079-*.md` and `079.*-*.md` returns ZERO hits; the highest existing phStaging2 story is 078. The only 079 anywhere under the stories tree belongs to a different project and is unrelated. Every occurrence was introduced by head commit `e1db0f1`, which is itself UNTAGGED (no `[story-NNN]` prefix); the delta base `3fb4e34` contains none. The work so attributed is the whole subject of this audit — the Phase 7.4 PhlimboV2→V3 cutover rehearsal, the local-only Kendu promotion, the keyless DepositPageViewV3 registration, the AddressLoader rewrite. It is also covered by no story that DOES exist: 076 and 077 scope themselves to mainnet `script/`/`src/` and never mention DeployMocks, and 078 explicitly instructs 'Do not modify `DeployMocks.s.sol`.' Related metadata flag: four of the seven closure stories closed via an undocumented `auto-complete` state carrying 'Approved by: story-batch workflow (machine approval — not human-reviewed)', including BOTH audit-remediation stories 074 and 075, and story 075's own declared primary regression gate (`npm run promotion-ready:dry`) was never run. IMPORTANTLY, this is a provenance gap and not a correctness gap: the work was verified to behave correctly on its own terms — stake conserved 300e18 through a chunked two-pass migration, V2 drained to 0, mint authority moved V2→V3, the two-step APY latch committed on both, the promo armed with four non-vacuous read-back requires, and DepositPageViewV3 registered and returning a live 23-field tuple. The code is unusually well commented and argues each divergence in place.
findings.impact: No behavioural impact. The cost is that a substantial, deliberately-divergent change to the project's only cutover rehearsal cannot be graded for story-faithfulness by anyone — including a future audit — because no acceptance criteria exist, and one story in scope actively forbids the change that was made. Under Law 2 that is reportable in itself.
findings.evidence: grep of 'Story 079' across script/ (11 hits); find over ~/code/product-owner/stories/phStaging2 for 079-*.md and 079.*-*.md (zero hits); git log showing e1db0f1 untagged; story 078 text; reports/.../script-audits/dev/closure-summary.md section 6
findings.recommendation: Write the missing story retrospectively and tag it, or re-attribute the work to a real story number and correct the eleven in-source references so they do not point at a document that does not exist. Separately, surface the `auto-complete` state in the story workflow's own documentation and re-review 074/075 by a human — an audit-remediation story that closed by machine approval, whose declared regression gate was never run, is the weakest link in the chain that this rehearsal exists to strengthen.
